In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the immunodominants of dextrans and levans are terminal or nonterminal depending on the antigenic determinant.
the terminal and nonterminal immunodeterminants in polysaccharides can be of a variety of structures.

immunoglobulins specific for terminal determinants in polysaccharide chains react only at the nonreducing end and those with nonterminal specificity can react along the chain at sites of nonreducing branch points or at nonterminal sites on the linear backbone.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the binding properties of immunoglobulins for oligosaccharide chains are determined by the immunodominance of certain groups and by the number and location of these groups along the chain.

immunoglobulins specific for terminal or for nonterminal determinants on dextran chains have been isolated and characterized and that the binding properties of these molecules have been defined quantitatively.

immunological reactions of polysaccharides are governed by the same principles that control the specificity of antibodies for proteins, namely, that the immunodominance of an antigenic determinant depends on its accessibility and the number of antigenic groups per molecule, and that the immunodeterminant is a small part of a much larger molecule.
The main takeaway from our work is that
terminal specificity and nonterminal specificity are two separate and distinct properties which can be found in the same molecule, and which are not related to one another by the size of the antigen.
the terminal nonreduced end of a polysaccharide chain is not always the most immunodominant site for antibody combining.

the immunodominance of the terminal nonreduced ends of dextran is a common feature of all antidextrans and that the nonterminal determinants on dextran are expressed by oligosaccharide sequences of three or more isomaltoside residues.
